newsitem.title: UK: Britain urges N.Ireland Protestans to heed "reason".
newsitem.headline: Britain urges N.Ireland Protestans to heed "reason".

text.p: British troops took up positions around the Northern Irish town of Portadown on Friday amid deadlock over plans by Protestants to stage a disputed march through a Roman Catholic neighbourhood.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, said no decision had yet been made on whether to ban or permit Sunday's Protestant Orange Order parade as tensions rose across the province.

She appealed to the order to "listen to the voice of reason" in a thinly-veiled reference to proposals by its leader, Grand Master Robert Saulters, to re-route a parade which last year sparked the worst civil violence in Northern Ireland in decades.

"Many in the Orange Order have shown some flexibility. For the good of everyone and for the sake of peace in the next few weeks, I urge those in the Portadown Orange to listen to those voices of reason," Mowlam told a hastily-convened news conference.
Her remarks made no reference to a Catholic residents association which opposes the march and were seen as a direct appeal to the Orange Order to call it off.

Hardline Orange Order members say such a decision would appease Catholic supporters of the Irish Republican Army guerrilla group, which has fought British rule for 28 years to reunite the province with the Irish republic.
Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, said the British government had a responsibility to Catholics opposed to the march.

"Host communities, which find particular marches objectionable, have the right to withhold their consent and to have their rights respected. The British government has a responsibility to uphold those rights," he said in a statement.
Last year police banned the parade until Protestant rioting forced a reversal of the decision, provoking a wave of Catholic fury and days of widespread civil disorder.
Mowlam said she would continue to seek a compromise between the pro-British Orange Order and Catholic Irish nationalists in the Garvaghy road who say the march past their homes is intimidation.
Portadown residents said columns of British troops and Northern Ireland police were taking up positions in and around the town.
Joel Patton, leader of a hardline Orange faction which opposes any modification of the route of march, said he felt sure the parade was now going to be banned by police.
"During the week I believed the parade would go ahead but since last night I believe there is...a change to stop the parade on Sunday," he told reporters in Portadown.
Local media said shops reported a run on frozen food, bottled water and gas cannisters by households worried that civil unrest might erupt anew and close roads and shops.
The banned Protestant Loyalist Volunteer Force, which has threatened to kill Catholics if the march is stopped, earlier admitted placing a hoax bomb in the Garvaghy Road enclave.

Orange leaders insist that the parade will be solemn and dignified. They say its aim is simply to celebrate their Protestant faith and commemorate Northern Ireland soldiers killed in the World War One Battle of the Somme.
